claims.text: Protective-oxide stability and integrity in CrFeCoNiX alloys are governed by the balance of the outward diffusivities of Cr and X.
Comparable, controlled diffusion rates of Cr and X produce a slow-growing oxide.
Comparable, controlled diffusion rates of Cr and X produce a coherent oxide.
For X = Al, the resulting protective scale is expected to be an Al2O3-rich mixed oxide.
CrFeCoNiAl is expected to have more balanced and controlled Cr and Al diffusion than the corresponding Si- or Mn-containing alloys.
Unbalanced diffusion of Cr and X causes rapid oxide buildup.
Rapid oxide buildup generates excessive internal stress in the scale.
High internal stress causes oxide-scale cracking or spallation.
Effective diffusion of Cr and X through both the alloy matrix and growing oxide determines scale growth rate and integrity.
A balance between the supply and outward diffusion of oxidizable elements permits slow, adherent oxide growth.
CrFeCoNiAl will form a slower-growing oxide layer than CrFeCoNiSi and CrFeCoNiMn.
CrFeCoNiAl will form a more coherent oxide layer than CrFeCoNiSi and CrFeCoNiMn.
CrFeCoNiSi and CrFeCoNiMn will exhibit faster oxide-scale growth than the baseline CrFeCoNi alloy.
CrFeCoNiSi and CrFeCoNiMn will exhibit greater scale stress and more cracking or spallation than the baseline CrFeCoNi alloy.
The proposed behavior applies to single-phase solid-solution CrFeCoNiX alloys exposed above 900 °C in oxidative or corrosive atmospheres.
Multiphase material states may deviate from the proposed relationship.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis identifies outward diffusion of Cr and X as the governing transport, whereas the mechanism refers to an inward supply of the same oxidizable elements being balanced with their outward diffusion. The transport directions and the physical meaning of this balance are therefore internally inconsistent or insufficiently distinguished.
